talk: Part 1: Do you have a large or a small family? Who are you closest to?
Part 2: Describe a relative you admire. Say who they are, what they are like, how often you see them, and explain why you admire them.
Part 3: Do you think the extended family is less important today than it was in the past? Why?

r.text:
Psychologists have long argued about how much of our character comes from nature and how much from our upbringing. Studies of siblings offer some of the clearest evidence. Brothers and sisters share roughly half of their genes, and most grow up in the same home, yet their temperaments are often strikingly different.

One explanation is sibling rivalry. Children compete for their parents' attention, and each child tends to find a different role in the family: one becomes the responsible one, another the joker. Over time these roles shape the way each person interacts with others outside the home as well.

The ties between siblings usually endure longer than any other relationship in life. Parents die, friendships break down, but a brother or sister can remain a connection to childhood for seventy years or more. Researchers in Scandinavia found that adults in close-knit families who saw their siblings regularly reported fewer feelings of loneliness in old age.

The extended family matters too. In many cultures grandparents play an active role in raising children, and family gatherings are where young people learn how to relate to people of every age. A stable upbringing, it seems, depends less on the size of the family than on the quality of the bonds within it.

Part 3: At what age do you think young people become mature? Does it depend on the person or on their culture?

r.text:
In the first year of life an infant's brain roughly doubles in size, and the speed of development in early childhood is hard to match at any later stage. Doctors describe this growth through milestones: the age at which a child first smiles, sits up, walks or says a word.

These milestones are useful, but parents are often reminded that every child develops at a different rate. One toddler may walk at nine months and another at fifteen, and both are perfectly normal. What matters more is that each phase follows the last in a typical order.

Cognitive skills grow alongside physical ones. Between the ages of two and four, children begin to imitate adults, use gestures to make themselves understood and start to master abstract concepts such as 'yesterday' and 'more'. Their imagination flourishes in play, and they gradually acquire the social skills they need to share and take turns with their peers.

The transition from toddler to schoolchild also brings emotional changes. A child who throws a tantrum at two will usually have learned, by five, to wait patiently and to express frustration in words. Bear in mind, however, that maturity is not a straight line: tired or ill children often return briefly to earlier behaviour.

script.t: All right, Arman. You've had a minute to prepare. Please describe a moment from your childhood that you remember well.
When I look back, the moment I remember most clearly is learning to ride a bike. I was about seven, and I was quite a clumsy child, so it took a long time.
Who taught you?
My grandfather. He was very patient. Every evening he would hold the back of the seat and run behind me. One day I realised he had let go and I was riding on my own. I was so proud.
Why do you think you remember it so well?
I think because it was a real milestone. It was the first time I felt independent. I still reminisce about it with my grandfather; it reminds us both how stubborn I was.
Thank you. Do you think children today have the same kind of experiences?
To some extent. But many children spend more time on screens, so they may master technology before they master a bike.

A balanced diet and regular exercise are widely recognised as vital for good health. Sleep, by contrast, is often the first thing people sacrifice when life becomes busy. Yet a growing body of research suggests that a persistent lack of sleep can be as harmful as a poor diet.

When adults sleep fewer than six hours a night for several weeks, levels of the hormones that control appetite are disrupted. People report stronger cravings for sugary and fatty foods, and their daily calorie intake rises. Over time this pattern may contribute to obesity and increase the risk of heart disease.

Chronic insomnia is also linked to anxiety and depression, though doctors stress that the relationship works in both directions: stress can trigger sleeplessness, and sleeplessness makes stress harder to manage.

The good news is that moderate changes can reverse much of the damage. A brisk walk in the afternoon, a fixed time for going to bed and avoiding screens for an hour before sleep all help the body recover its natural rhythm. Dieticians also recommend eating the largest portion of the day at lunch rather than late in the evening. Such habits cannot cure every condition, but they are a simple way to reduce the risk of many.

r.text:
Economists in the twentieth century predicted that technology would free people from work, leaving them with long hours of leisure. In many countries the opposite has happened. Surveys show that professionals now spend more time working than their parents did, and many say they find it difficult to achieve a balance between their job and their private life.

Part of the reason is the rising cost of living. When housing and living expenses increase, people work longer hours simply to maintain their standard of living. Another reason is attitude. For a growing number of people, work is no longer just a way to make a living but the main source of fulfilment and identity.

However, there are signs of change. In a recent national survey, over half of respondents under thirty said they would accept a lower salary in exchange for more free time. They described leisure not as a luxury but as a priority: time for hobbies, creativity and self-expression.

Optimists see this as a healthy shift in outlook. Pessimists warn that it may only apply to the wealthy, who can afford to choose. People from all walks of life, they argue, should have the opportunity to live life to the full, not only those with savings.

Supervision. Every Masters and PhD student is assigned a tutor who supervises their research. You should meet your tutor at least once a fortnight in the first term. Bring a short written summary of your progress to each meeting.

r.text:
Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, but nearly half of them may vanish by the end of this century. A language dies when the last person who speaks it as a mother tongue passes away, and in many communities that day is not far off.

The causes are rarely sudden. In most cases parents choose to raise their children in a more widely spoken language because they believe it will offer better jobs and education. Within two or three generations, the original language is used only by elderly people, and the young can comprehend it but no longer converse in it.

Why does this matter? Each language contains vocabulary and concepts that other languages lack. Some languages have dozens of words for types of snow or for kinds of family relationship, and these words illustrate how speakers see the world. When a language is lost, that knowledge is lost with it.

There are, however, success stories. Welsh, once in decline, is now taught in every school in Wales, and the number of young fluent speakers has risen. Revival programmes demonstrate that a language can survive, but only if communities, schools and governments act together and early.

script.t: Good afternoon. Today I'd like to look at how infants acquire their first language.
Even before birth, babies can distinguish their mother's voice from other voices. Within days, they prefer the sound of their own language.
Between six and ten months, babies begin to babble. Interestingly, at first babies around the world babble in very similar ways.
By about twelve months, most children produce their first word. Gestures, such as pointing, are an important step towards this.
The next stage is often called the vocabulary explosion. At around eighteen months, a child may learn ten new words a day.
It's important to note that children don't simply imitate adults. They make mistakes such as 'I goed', which shows they are working out rules for themselves.
Finally, research suggests that the quantity of conversation matters. Children whose parents talk with them, rather than at them, develop larger vocabularies.
Next week we'll consider what happens when a child grows up with two languages.

Archaeologists rely on several methods to date the objects they find. The simplest is to study the layers of soil at an excavation site. In general, deeper layers are older, so an object found below another usually predates it. This gives a chronological order, but not an exact date.

For more precise dating, scientists use radiocarbon dating. All living things absorb carbon, and after death a form of it decays at a known rate. By measuring how much remains in bone, wood or seeds, researchers can calculate when the organism died, as far back as about fifty thousand years.

Tree rings provide another timeline. Each year a tree adds a ring, and the width varies with the climate. By matching patterns from many trees, scientists have built records that span more than twelve thousand years. Wooden beams from historical buildings can be dated to the exact year the tree was cut.

None of these methods is perfect. Soil can be disturbed by animals or by later digging, and samples can be contaminated. For this reason, archaeologists prefer to infer a date only when two or more independent methods give consistent results.

script.t: In today's lecture we'll trace the history of timekeeping, from ancient civilisations to the present.
The earliest clocks were shadow clocks, used in Egypt around 1500 BC. Their obvious weakness was that they were useless at night or on cloudy days.
Water clocks solved this problem. Water dripped from one container to another at a steady rate, and the level showed how much time had passed.
In the Middle Ages, mechanical clocks appeared in European towns. They were large, placed in church towers, and often lost as much as fifteen minutes a day.
A major step came in 1656, when the pendulum clock was invented. It reduced errors to less than a minute a day.
Then, in the twentieth century, quartz and later atomic clocks made timekeeping extraordinarily precise. An atomic clock loses about one second in a hundred million years.
Prior to the railways, every town kept its own local time. Standard time zones were introduced so that train timetables made sense.
Next week we'll discuss the calendar.

r.text:
When a species is introduced to a new habitat, the results can be catastrophic. Without the predators and diseases that kept its numbers down at home, an introduced animal or plant can multiply rapidly and threaten native species.

Australia offers some of the best-known examples. Rabbits, brought by European settlers in the nineteenth century, spread across the continent within fifty years. They destroyed vegetation, caused severe soil erosion and competed with native animals for food. Cane toads, introduced in 1935 to control insects that damaged sugar crops, proved even worse. They failed to control the insects, and because they are poisonous, they killed many native predators that tried to eat them.

Islands are especially vulnerable. Species that evolved in isolation often have no defence against newcomers, and many of the world's recent extinctions have occurred on islands after rats or cats arrived on ships.

Today, many countries have strict rules to stop new species entering. Where invaders are already established, governments try to eradicate them or at least reduce their numbers, but this is expensive and rarely completely successful. Ecologists agree that prevention is far cheaper than cure.

r.text:
Since the first space station was launched in 1971, hundreds of astronauts have lived and worked in orbit around the Earth. Their experience has taught scientists a great deal about how the human body responds to weightlessness.

Without gravity, fluids in the body move towards the head, which is why astronauts often look puffy in photographs. Muscles weaken because they no longer have to support the body, and bones can lose up to one percent of their mass each month. To counter this, crew members exercise for about two hours every day on specially designed machines.

Radiation is another danger. Outside the protection of the Earth's atmosphere, astronauts are exposed to far higher levels than on the surface. Long missions therefore carry a greater risk of cancer in later life.

Psychological pressures matter too. Crew members live in a confined space with the same small group for months. Before a mission, they train in simulators and isolation experiments on Earth so that they can acclimatise to these conditions.

If humans are ever to colonise the Moon or travel to Mars, these problems must be solved. A return trip to Mars could take nearly three years, much longer than any astronaut has yet spent in space.

For most of the twentieth century, tall buildings meant steel and concrete. Timber was considered suitable only for cottages and single-storey houses. Today, however, engineers are designing multi-storey residences made almost entirely of wood.

The key innovation is cross-laminated timber: layers of wood glued together at right angles to form panels as strong as concrete. These panels are prefabricated in a factory and lifted into place on site, so construction is faster and quieter. A ten-storey apartment block in London was built in just twelve weeks.

Supporters argue that timber is the most sustainable structural material. Producing cement and steel releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, whereas trees absorb carbon as they grow. If forests are managed responsibly, wood is also renewable.

Critics raise concerns about fire. Engineers respond that thick timber panels burn slowly and predictably, forming a protective layer of charcoal on the exterior, and that modern designs include sprinklers and fire-resistant staircases.

Occupants of these buildings often describe them as warm, airy and spacious. Whether timber will replace concrete in the skyscrapers of the future remains to be seen, but it is no longer seen as old-fashioned.

r.text:
Twenty years ago, the idea of talking to your fridge would have seemed like science fiction. Today millions of homes contain devices that connect to the Internet and to each other. Lights, heating, door locks and even washing machines can be operated by remote control from a smartphone.

Manufacturers present these gadgets as labour-saving and user-friendly. A thermostat that learns when its owners are at home, for example, can reduce heating bills by around ten percent. For elderly or disabled people, voice-controlled devices can make everyday life considerably more independent.

However, the technology raises serious questions. Every connected device collects data about the habits of the people who use it, and this information is stored on company servers. Security experts have shown that poorly protected devices can be hacked, and in some cases cameras have been accessed by strangers.

There is also the problem of products quickly becoming dated. A device that is state-of-the-art today may stop receiving software updates in five years, leaving owners with an expensive object that no longer works properly.

Most analysts expect smart homes to become the norm. The challenge for governments is to ensure that convenience does not come at the cost of privacy.

r.text:
By 2050, around two-thirds of the world's population is expected to live in cities. In developing countries the speed of urbanisation is staggering: some cities double in size in less than twenty years. Rapid growth brings economic benefits, but it also presents pressing challenges.

The most visible problem is housing. When migrants from rural areas arrive faster than decent homes can be built, slums grow on the edges of the city. Residents often lack adequate water, sanitation and electricity. Traffic congestion is another issue: as car ownership rises, journeys that once took twenty minutes may take two hours.

Some cities have found creative ways to tackle these problems. Curitiba in Brazil introduced a cheap and efficient bus system in the 1970s that is still copied around the world. Singapore built large amounts of public housing and now houses around eighty percent of its population in government-built flats. Medellín in Colombia connected hillside neighbourhoods to the centre with cable cars, which reduced journey times and helped to include communities that had been isolated.

These examples show that short-term solutions are rarely enough. Successful cities think long-term, invest in infrastructure early and involve residents in decisions.

r.text:
The diagram illustrates the process by which used plastic bottles are recycled into new products.

Overall, there are six main stages, beginning with the collection of waste bottles and ending with the manufacture of new items such as clothing and containers.

First, used bottles are collected from households and recycling bins and transported to a sorting plant. There, they are sorted by type and colour, and any bottles that cannot be recycled are removed. Next, the bottles are washed thoroughly to eliminate labels, glue and other contaminants.

After washing, the clean bottles are fed into a machine which shreds them into small flakes. These flakes are then heated until they melt, and the liquid plastic is formed into tiny pellets.

At the final stage, the pellets are sold to manufacturers, who use them to make a range of products, including polyester fabric, carpets and new bottles. The cycle can then begin again.

script.t: Today I want to look at one of the most pervasive pollutants on the planet: plastic in the oceans.
It's estimated that around eight million tonnes of plastic enter the oceans every year. Most of it comes from land, carried by rivers.
Large items are a threat to wildlife. Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed pieces to their chicks.
But the greater long-term problem may be microplastics: tiny fragments less than five millimetres long. These enter the food chain and have been found in fish, salt and even drinking water.
Can the damage be reversed? Cleaning the open ocean is extremely difficult and, many scientists argue, largely futile while plastic keeps entering the water.
The most viable solution is to stop plastic reaching the sea in the first place. That means better waste management in coastal cities and reducing single-use plastics.
Several countries have already banned plastic bags, and the results are encouraging.
For next week, please read the article on biodegradable materials.

In 2010, electric vehicles were a curiosity. Today they account for a significant share of new car sales in many countries, and some governments plan to ban new petrol cars within the next decade.

The main argument for electric cars is that they emit no exhaust fumes. In crowded cities, where air pollution causes serious health problems, this is a clear benefit. However, the overall effect on carbon emissions depends on how the electricity is produced. In a country that relies on coal, an electric car may be responsible for almost as much carbon dioxide as an efficient petrol car.

Batteries are another issue. They require metals such as lithium and cobalt, which are expensive to extract and whose mining can damage the environment. Researchers are developing new types of rechargeable battery that use more common materials, and recycling programmes aim to recover valuable metals from old batteries.

Cost has been the biggest barrier for consumers, but prices are falling steadily. Analysts predict that within a few years an electric car will cost no more to buy than a conventional one, and much less to run. If renewable energy continues to grow, the benefits of electric vehicles are likely to outweigh the drawbacks.

Question: Some people believe that job satisfaction is more important than a high salary. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

In today's competitive job market, many people face a choice between a well-paid but demanding job and a less profitable career that they genuinely enjoy. While a good income is clearly necessary, I believe that job satisfaction is ultimately more important.

Admittedly, money matters. Employees need to earn enough to cover the cost of living, and a higher salary allows people to support their families and save for retirement. For workers in low-paid or casual employment, financial security may understandably be the main priority.

Nevertheless, once basic needs are met, research suggests that additional income has a limited effect on happiness. People who find their work rewarding tend to be more motivated and more productive, and they are less likely to suffer from stress. By contrast, a monotonous job, however well paid, can lead to exhaustion and dissatisfaction.

Furthermore, satisfying work often leads to better prospects in the long term. Employees who enjoy what they do are more likely to develop new skills and be promoted.

In conclusion, although a reasonable salary is essential, I am convinced that job satisfaction plays a greater role in a fulfilling working life.

Most societies use imprisonment as the main punishment for serious crime. The aims are to punish the offender, to protect the public and to deter others from committing similar offences. Increasingly, however, criminologists ask whether prison achieves these aims, particularly for non-violent offenders.

Figures from several European countries suggest that more than half of prisoners reoffend within two years of release. Prison removes people from their families and jobs, and inmates may learn new criminal skills from other prisoners. For petty crimes such as minor theft or vandalism, critics argue, imprisonment can make the problem worse.

Alternatives include community service, electronic monitoring and programmes that bring offenders face to face with their victims. In Norway, which has one of the lowest reoffending rates in Europe, prisons focus on education and training so that prisoners can find work after release.

Supporters of harsh sentences reply that strict punishment is what victims and the public expect, and that some offenders are simply too dangerous to release. Most experts agree that prison is necessary for violent criminals; the debate is about how to deal with the rest.

Question: More and more people now get their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Over the past decade, social media has become a major source of news, particularly for young people. While this development has clear benefits, I believe the disadvantages are more significant.

On the one hand, social media gives people immediate access to current affairs. Events are reported as they happen, often by eyewitnesses, and users can follow a wide range of sources rather than relying on one newspaper. In countries where the press is controlled, social media can also expose stories that mainstream outlets ignore.

On the other hand, the information is often unreliable. Anyone can publish a post, and false or distorted stories frequently spread faster than accurate ones. Furthermore, the algorithms that decide what users see tend to show them content that matches their existing views, which can make people less well-informed and more biased. Finally, sensationalist headlines designed to attract attention often replace serious, investigative journalism.

In conclusion, although social media makes news faster and more diverse, the risks to accuracy and balance outweigh these advantages. Users need to verify what they read and support trusted sources of journalism.

In 2001 the British government abolished entrance fees at national museums. In the following decade, visits to the museums that had previously charged rose by more than one hundred and fifty percent. Supporters claim this proves that free entry makes culture accessible to people from all walks of life.

The picture is more complicated, however. Studies show that most of the additional visits were made by people who already visited museums regularly, rather than by new audiences. Groups that rarely visit galleries, such as young people from low-income families, often say that price is not the main barrier. Instead, they feel that museums are 'not for people like us'.

For this reason, many institutions now focus on making their exhibitions more interactive and relevant. Some invite local communities to help choose which artefacts are displayed, and others host evening events with live music and performances. These initiatives aim to change the atmosphere of the gallery from silent and formal to stimulating and welcoming.

Free entry also has a cost. Without ticket income, museums depend on government funding and private donations, which can fall when the economy is weak. Nevertheless, most visitors believe that a nation's art and history should belong to everyone, and few politicians would now dare to bring the fees back.

23.title: Academic Writing Task 1: data and processes
words: to increase suddenly and strongly in a short period
Applications to engineering courses began to surge in 2015, almost doubling within two years.
surge to + figure; surge in demand
Band 7+: Noun use is elegant: 'a surge in applications was recorded in 2015'.
to fall very quickly and by a large amount
Coal consumption went on to plummet after 2010, losing more than half its share.
plummet to + figure; plummet by + amount
Band 7+: Stronger than 'fall sharply'; avoid repeating it more than once per report.
a period when a figure stops changing after rising or falling
After a decade of growth, car ownership reached a plateau of around 450 vehicles per thousand people.
reach a plateau; hit a plateau at + figure
Band 7+: Also a verb: 'figures plateaued at 40%'.
to rise and fall irregularly over a period
Visitor numbers continued to fluctuate between 2 and 3 million throughout the 1990s.
fluctuate between X and Y; fluctuate wildly
Band 7+: Use 'erratic fluctuations' as a noun-based Band 8 alternative.
to rise very quickly to a high level
Online retail sales soared to a record 27% of total spending in 2021.

a small, usually temporary, fall in a figure
A brief dip in rail usage in 2009 was followed by a sustained recovery.
a slight dip in; a temporary dip
Band 7+: Pair with 'brief' or 'temporary' to show the fall did not last.

Tourist arrivals rebounded sharply in 2022, almost returning to pre-pandemic levels.
Band 7+: More precise than 'go up again'; also a noun: 'a strong rebound'.
a gradual decrease in amount, number or quality
The chart shows a steady decline in the proportion of households with landline phones.
a steady decline in; a decline of + figure
Band 7+: 'Decline in' = topic; 'decline of' = amount: 'a decline of 12%'.
to stop rising or falling and remain at a similar level

to reach the lowest point before starting to improve

Band 7+: Alternative: 'hit a low of' + figure.
a general pattern of increase over time
Electricity generated from wind power displayed an upward trend across the entire period.
show/display an upward trend; a clear upward trend
Band 7+: Band 8 variation: 'followed an upward trajectory'.
a continuing path of decrease over time

at a gradual, regular and continuous rate

Band 7+: More precise and formal than 'a bit'.
very suddenly and by a large amount

large in size, amount or importance

a substantial increase/rise; a substantial proportion

sudden and large, especially of a rise or fall

a sharp rise/fall/drop; a sharp contrast
neither very large nor very small

by a large or noticeable amount

slightly less than the stated figure

considerably more than the stated figure

compared with/to + noun; as compared with

used to contrast two facts in one sentence

Band 7+: Conjunction; 'while' is a slightly less formal alternative.
double the number of countable things

twice as many + plural noun + as

Band 7+: Opposite: 'the lowest proportion'; synonym: 'the largest share'.

Band 7+: Fractions add variety; avoid repeating raw percentages.
a very small part of something

Band 7+: Often used with 'the remainder': 'the remainder accounted for 10%'.

more than half of a group

Band 7+: 'The vast majority' emphasises a very large share.

Band 7+: Place at the end of the clause; saves space in comparisons.
The leaves are dried in the sun and subsequently ground into a fine powder.
Band 7+: More formal than 'after that'; vary with 'following this'.

Band 7+: Passive voice is standard in process descriptions.
as soon as; after something happens

at the last step of a process

the cycle begins/repeats; a closed cycle
Band 7+: Used for life cycles and recycling processes.
is changed into a different form

Overall, studying took up the most time in every age group, while sport accounted for the least. Time spent on social media rose steadily with age until the 18–21 group, where it levelled off.

24.title: Academic Writing Task 2: argument and cohesion
words: in addition; used to add a further point
Furthermore, remote work reduces commuting time, which benefits both employees and the environment.
Band 7+: Use at the start of a sentence; do not overuse in one paragraph.
Moreover, public transport investment can reduce inequality between urban districts.
Band 7+: Signals the added point is stronger than the previous one.
despite what has just been said
Fast food is convenient; nevertheless, its long-term health costs are considerable.
in an opposite way to what has just been described
Conversely, rural communities often lack access to specialist healthcare.
Band 7+: Use only when the second idea is genuinely opposite.
Many young people cannot afford housing; consequently, they live with their parents longer.
Band 7+: More formal than 'so'; synonym: 'as a consequence'.
as a result of the action just mentioned
Governments could tax sugary drinks, thereby discouraging excessive consumption.
Band 7+: Elegant; always followed by an -ing form.
Some cities operate a scheme whereby residents receive credits for recycling.
Band 7+: Formal relative adverb for systems and arrangements.
In addition to financial benefits, volunteering develops valuable social skills.
Band 7+: Followed by a noun or -ing, never a full clause.
used to introduce a contrasting point of view
On the other hand, strict censorship may limit artistic freedom.

Band 7+: Do not use 'on the one hand' without this second half.
Similarly, tourism can damage fragile ecosystems if it is poorly managed.
used to state an opinion that can be supported

Band 7+: Softens strong claims without sounding weak.
used to present a possible view cautiously

Band 7+: Stronger than 'may'; still appropriately cautious.

I am firmly convinced that university education should remain free.

there is a strong case for

there is a strong case for + noun/-ing
Band 7+: Opposite: 'there is little justification for'.

used to accept that something is true before arguing

Band 7+: Slightly more formal than 'due to'.

Band 7+: More precise than 'such as'; lists all items.
as shown by a particular example

to improve the quality or value of something

Band 7+: Formal substitute for 'get rid of'.
to make a problem less serious

Band 7+: Uses the subjunctive: 'that they act', not 'acts'.

Band 7+: Not 'with regards to' in formal writing.
